turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, thank you for fitting me in. I... I suppose I should give you a little context first so you understand where I am coming from. I’m a secondary school teacher, and I have been for quite some time, so I am very used to the daily rhythms of a school, you know, the administrative side of things, the constant communication. But lately, I’ve been dealing with something that I just can’t seem to get past, which is why I’m here. 

It really centers around the morning routine. I came in today because I simply cannot shake this intense feeling that certain staff emails and the daily morning announcements are... well, that they are actually coded messages about me. I know how unusual that might sound to say out loud. But when I sit at my desk before first period and read through the administration’s updates, the specific phrasing they use just feels so deeply personal, like there is a hidden meaning intended only for me to understand. And the announcements over the loudspeaker, the way certain words are emphasized by the principal... it just feels directed right at me, wrapped up in ordinary school business. 

My colleagues have been very sweet about it, very gentle. A few of them have even pulled up the emails on their own computers and sat down with me to show me the recipient list, trying to prove that the exact same message was sent to every single teacher in the building. And I see it, I look right at the screen and see that it went to everyone, but... I just can't shake the feeling. The feeling doesn't go away just because the mailing list is long, you know? It just sits with me all day while I'm trying to teach my classes, this nagging certainty that the message was really just for me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a fixed belief that staff emails and morning announcements contain coded messages directed at them, which persists even when colleagues provide contradictory evidence showing the messages were sent to everyone.

turns.doctor_question: Have you heard any voices that other people could not hear?
turns.patient_response:
Voices... well, it’s interesting that you bring that up, because I have been noticing something along those lines, and I’ve really been going back and forth on whether or not to even mention it. You see, during the school day, it is just so incredibly loud. There’s the bell, the lockers slamming, the teenagers shouting down the halls... you barely have a single moment to hear yourself think, let alone hear anything else. 

But it’s when things finally settle down that I notice it. Usually, it happens after the final bell rings and my classroom empties out. The kids rush off to catch their buses, and I’m just sitting there at my desk, maybe wiping down the whiteboard or organizing my lesson plans for the next day, and the room is completely quiet. Or even later, when I’m finally back at my house, just in the absolute quiet of my own kitchen while I'm grading papers or putting the kettle on for a cup of tea. 

In those very still, quiet moments... I will hear a woman’s voice. It’s not a mumble or a whisper, it is perfectly clear. She’ll just say my name, or she might make a very brief, short comment about exactly what I’m doing right then in that exact moment. And it is so incredibly vivid, so real, that my immediate reflex is to reply. I actually speak out loud and answer her! I'll say, "Yes, I'm over here," or "I know, I'm just finishing up," before it suddenly dawns on me that the door is shut, the house or the classroom is completely empty, and there is absolutely no one else there with me. It’s just so disorienting because of how perfectly ordinary and clear the voice sounds, you know? I always end up getting up from my desk and checking the hallway or looking out the window just to be absolutely sure, but... there's never anyone there.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly describes hearing a clear, vivid woman's voice speaking to them when they are completely alone, confirming auditory hallucinations.

Well, that's... I mean, I've really been trying to keep a close eye on my moods, you know, just as a general practice, because teaching takes so much out of you emotionally anyway. You have to be "on" all the time for the students. But as for feeling unusually depressed, or... or energized, like you said... no, I really don't think so. I haven't noticed anything like that. 

I mean, I get tired, of course. By Friday afternoon, I am just absolutely wiped out, but that's just the nature of the job, isn't it? Grading fifty essays over the weekend will drain anyone. And I certainly don't have periods where I feel overly energized or "up," as you put it. I'm actually a very steady person, very even-keeled. I've always been that way, which is why these... these other things, the emails and the voice, are so distressing to me, because they just don't fit into my normal, predictable routine. I wake up at the same time, I go to work, I come home, I make my tea... my energy levels and my mood just stay very consistent through all of it. I'm not crying all the time or feeling hopeless, and I'm definitely not bouncing off the walls with energy. It's just... I'm just me, just my normal self, except for these very specific, very strange things happening around me.

turns.doctor_question: How old were you when these experiences first started?
turns.patient_response:
Well, let me think back, because I really want to give you an accurate timeline, and it’s a bit tricky to pinpoint the exact day it all began, you know? I’m fifty-six now, and I’ve been teaching for over thirty years, so I have a very long, very stable history of just going about my business, managing my classrooms, and dealing with the administration without a second thought. I mean, I’ve been through six different principals in my career, so I know how these things usually go. 

But as for when this specific feeling started—the certainty about the coded messages in the emails and the announcements, and then, of course, the voice that I hear in the quiet moments when I'm just sitting at my desk or making my tea... I’d say all of that really started about four months ago. 

I remember it was right around the time the first quarter grades were due, which is always a very hectic time of year anyway. At first, I thought maybe I was just overthinking things because of the stress of getting all the reports filed on time. You know how it is, your brain gets a bit scrambled when you’re staring at spreadsheets for hours on end. But then the quarter ended, the grades were submitted, and the stress died down, but the feelings didn't. The emails kept coming, and they kept feeling so pointed, so specific to me. And the voice... well, that hasn't gone away either. So yes, I've been fifty-six this whole time, and it's been a solid four months of dealing with this day in and day out. It’s just so strange, because for fifty-five and a half years, I never experienced anything even remotely like this.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a certainty that emails and announcements contain coded messages specifically pointed at them, indicating referential delusions.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly mentions hearing a voice during quiet moments that has persisted for four months, indicating auditory hallucinations.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any problems with your memory or concentration?
turns.patient_response:
Memory or concentration... well, it's funny you ask that, because as a teacher, I am constantly having to evaluate other people's memory and concentration, you know? I'm always telling my students, "Pay attention, focus on the text, remember what we discussed on Tuesday," so I'm very hyper-aware of cognitive slips. I have to be. I have to keep track of thirty teenagers at a time, remember who has a 504 plan, who needs extra time on tests, who is allergic to peanuts... it's a lot to juggle.

But as for my own memory and concentration? No, I really haven't noticed any issues there at all. I mean, my mind feels as sharp as it ever has. I can still sit down and grade a stack of essays and spot a comma splice from a mile away. I remember all my lesson plans, I know exactly where I left off in the curriculum, and I haven't forgotten any appointments or misplaced my keys or anything like that. 

I will say, though, that the... the distractions, the voice and the emails, they certainly demand my attention. When you're sitting in a quiet room and you hear someone say your name as clear as day, it's impossible not to stop what you're doing and focus on that. So, in that exact moment, my concentration on whatever I was doing—grading, reading, making tea—is interrupted. But it's not because I've lost the ability to concentrate. It's because something very startling has just happened and pulled my focus away. Once I realize no one is there, I can sit right back down and pick up exactly where I left off. So, no, my memory is perfectly fine, and my concentration is just as good as it always is, assuming I'm not being interrupted by... well, by these things.

turns.doctor_question: Have you had any recent head injury, seizure, stroke, or other major medical problem before these symptoms began?
turns.patient_response:
Well, a head injury? Or a stroke? Goodness, no. I mean, I really try to take excellent care of myself, as much as one can when they spend nine months out of the year in a building full of walking petri dishes—teenagers are just constantly passing around colds and the flu, you know. But I've always been very diligent about my health. I get my annual checkups, I take my vitamins, I try to get my steps in during my lunch break by walking the perimeter of the athletic fields if the weather is nice. 

But as for anything major like a seizure or a stroke... absolutely not. I haven't hit my head, I haven't been in any accidents. The most medical trouble I've had in the last five years was a mild case of plantar fasciitis from wearing the wrong shoes on concrete floors all day, and I got orthotic inserts for that and it cleared right up. 

I've never been hospitalized for anything serious, never had surgery... I mean, I had my tonsils out when I was seven, but I hardly think that counts, does it? My blood pressure is always right in the normal range when I go to Dr. Evans—he's my primary care physician, I've been seeing him for about fifteen years now. He always tells me I'm wonderfully boring, medically speaking. So no, there was absolutely nothing physical that happened before these four months. No sudden illnesses, no fainting spells, no neurological events. Just... my perfectly ordinary, healthy life, right up until the emails started feeling so strange and the voice began. So I really don't think there's a medical, or physical, explanation for this, if that's what you're getting at. It's just my body is perfectly fine, it's just these other things that are happening.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly mentions that 'the voice began', indicating the presence of auditory hallucinations.

turns.doctor_question: Do you feel as though anyone or anything is controlling your thoughts, feelings, or actions?
turns.patient_response:
Well, controlling my thoughts or actions... no, I wouldn't say that anyone is controlling me. I still make my own decisions, I still grade my papers, I still choose what tea to drink. I'm very much in control of myself. But... and this is the part that really made me realize I needed to talk to someone, because it's just so unsettling... I do feel like I'm being targeted, or maybe not targeted, but spoken to, in a very specific, hidden way. 

It's the emails from the administration, mostly. And the morning announcements over the PA system. I know how it sounds, believe me, I do. But I just can't shake this profound feeling that there are coded messages in them, and that they are specifically about me. 

For instance, last week, the principal sent out a completely standard email to the entire staff about keeping the hallways clear during passing periods. Very routine, right? But the way certain words were phrased, the specific cadence of the sentences... it felt like a direct commentary on how I had been standing outside my door during third period. It felt like a warning, or a message meant only for my eyes, disguised as a mass email. 

And I've tried to be rational about it. I really have. I even sat down with Mrs. Gable—she teaches history across the hall, we've been friends for years—and I showed her the email. I pointed out the phrasing, and she very gently, very kindly, pulled up the exact same email on her own computer to show me that it went to everyone, word for word. She tried to assure me it was just a general reminder. And intellectually, looking at her screen, I understood what she was saying. But the feeling... that absolute certainty that the message was secretly meant for me, that it was a code I was supposed to decipher... it just wouldn't go away. It hasn't gone away. It's like I'm living in two different realities—the one where it's a normal school day, and the one where the announcements are narrating my life. But no, to answer your question directly, they aren't controlling my actions. They're just... communicating with me. Or about me. And it's exhausting trying to read between the lines of every single staff memo.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes clear referential delusions, believing that routine mass emails and school announcements contain hidden, coded messages specifically directed at them, and this belief persists despite contradictory evidence from a colleague.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any trouble keeping up with your work or daily responsibilities because of these experiences?
turns.patient_response:
Well, trouble keeping up... it's a complicated question, really. Because on paper, if you look at my attendance record or my grade book, I am still teaching. I haven't taken a leave of absence, I haven't called in sick... I am there every morning at 7:15, unlocking my door, turning on the smartboard, writing the day's objective on the whiteboard. I'm physically present, and I'm still delivering the curriculum. 

But... and this is hard to admit, because I pride myself on being very self-sufficient, very capable... I have had to lean on my colleagues a lot more than I usually do. Especially with the bigger project lessons. Normally, I love those. I love the chaos of thirty kids working in groups, researching, debating. But lately, with the... the emails, and the feeling that I need to be constantly monitoring the announcements and the memos for these hidden messages... the noise of a project day is just too much. It's overwhelming. So I've had to ask Mrs. Gable, and sometimes Mr. Harrison from the science department, to come in during their planning periods and just... co-facilitate, I guess you'd call it. Just to help me keep all the plates spinning while my mind is, frankly, preoccupied with trying to decipher what the administration is really saying to me. And the planning meetings, the departmental ones we have on Wednesday afternoons? I used to lead those, or at least be a very active participant. Now, I find myself just sitting there, nodding, letting other people make the decisions about the pacing guide, because I'm just so drained from trying to read between the lines of the agenda.

And outside of school... well, that's where things have really slipped, I suppose. I've always been very involved in my community. I've been in the same book club for eight years—we meet on the second Tuesday of every month, we rotate hosting, I usually make my famous lemon bars. But the last three months, I've just... cancelled. I haven't even read the books. I just couldn't focus on fiction when there were so many real, urgent messages I needed to figure out. I haven't been volunteering with the community theater like I usually do in the spring, and I missed the neighborhood block party planning committee entirely. I just... I don't have the bandwidth for it anymore. I'm spending so much energy just trying to get through the school day and manage these... communications... that by the time the final bell rings, I just want to go home, lock the door, and be somewhere quiet. So, yes, I suppose you could say my responsibilities have taken a hit, even if I'm technically still showing up for work.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes referential delusions, believing there are hidden messages directed at them in emails, announcements, and meeting agendas.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed becoming more socially withdrawn or emotionally flat since these experiences began?
turns.patient_response:
Emotionally flat... well, that’s a rather harsh way to put it, isn't it? It sounds so cold, and I want to be very clear that I am not a cold person. I still care about my students, immensely. I care about whether they understand the reading, I care about their futures, I worry about the ones who sit in the back and don't take notes. And my friends, too—I still care very deeply for my friends. 

But... well, the best way I can describe it is that for many months now, it has just felt like the warmth and the drive have completely drained out of me. Just entirely siphoned away. It’s like a battery that’s been left out in the winter, if you know what I mean. The structure is all still there, but there's no spark left to power anything. 

So, yes, I suppose withdrawn is accurate, because I just let things go. I mentioned the book club earlier, and the community theater planning... I didn't formally resign from them, I just let them slide. I stopped showing up. And it’s not just those big commitments, either, the ones that take a lot of work. It’s even simple things, like phone calls. My sister, Brenda, she calls me from Ohio every Sunday evening, regular as clockwork. We've done this for a decade. But lately, I just sit on my sofa and watch her name flash on the caller ID until it goes to voicemail. I just don't have the... the whatever it is you need inside you to pick up the receiver and make conversation about her garden or her grandchildren. 

I just let it all slide unless someone pushes me. If Mrs. Gable doesn't physically come to my classroom at noon and say, "Come on, we are going to the staff room for lunch," I will just sit at my desk in the quiet, eating half a sandwich and staring at the wall. If someone doesn't prompt me, if someone doesn't pull me into the current, I just drift. The caring is still in my head, I know I love these people and these activities, but the actual drive to participate in my own life is just... gone.

symptom_reasoning.S023: The patient describes a profound loss of drive (avolition) and social withdrawal (asociality), noting they let commitments slide and only engage if prompted by others.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient confirms social withdrawal and a loss of motivation, having stopped attending their book club and community theater planning.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any change in your emotions, like feeling less able to express them or feeling emotionally flat?

Well, as I was just saying a moment ago—and I know "emotionally flat" is the phrase you're leaning toward, though I still struggle with how clinical and cold that sounds—it really does tie right back into what I was trying to explain about the warmth and the drive just completely draining out of me.

I just won't do it. I need that external push now, because my own internal emotional drive is just... it's just gone.

turns.doctor_question: Have you started, stopped, or changed any medications, supplements, or recreational substances around the time these symptoms began?
turns.patient_response:
Well, no. No, certainly not. I am a creature of habit, doctor, through and through, especially when it comes to my health and my routine. I haven't started anything new, and I certainly haven't stopped anything. I take my daily multivitamin—the same brand, the silver kind for women over fifty, I've been taking that exact one since my fiftieth birthday—and I take a standard calcium supplement every morning with my orange juice. That routine is absolutely set in stone. 

I haven't added any new herbal things or strange vitamins, either. My sister, Brenda, the one in Ohio I mentioned earlier? She is always reading these health blogs online and trying to mail me things... oh, ashwagandha or turmeric gummies, or whatever the latest fad is, telling me they'll give me more energy or help me feel more engaged. But I always tell her, "Brenda, I don't want to be messing with my system with unregulated supplements." I just don't trust them. So those bottles just sit in the back of my pantry, still sealed. I haven't touched them. 

And as for recreational substances... well, heavens, absolutely not. I'm a high school teacher! I am the one giving the teenagers lectures on why they shouldn't be vaping in the lavatories or experimenting with whatever they find at weekend parties. I take that responsibility as a role model very seriously. I don't even drink much to begin with—maybe half a glass of white wine on a holiday or at a nice dinner—but I haven't even had that in months because, as I was explaining, I haven't been going to my book club or any neighborhood gatherings anyway. So, no, my medicine cabinet and what I put into my body are exactly the same as they were a year ago, two years ago. Not a single change or addition to speak of.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever found it hard to keep your thoughts or speech organized, or do you usually speak clearly and stay on track?
turns.patient_response:
Well, no, I wouldn't say I have trouble keeping my thoughts organized. I mean, as a teacher, you really can't afford to lose your train of thought, can you? If you stand up in front of a room full of sixteen-year-olds and start rambling or losing your place, they will absolutely eat you alive. They notice everything. So I’ve always prided myself on being very articulate, very structured in how I present information. I have my lesson plans, I have my bullet points on the whiteboard, and I move from A to B to C very logically. 

And even now, with everything feeling so... drained, as I was describing earlier, my mind itself still feels perfectly sharp in that regard. When I do speak, when I do manage to muster the energy to actually have a conversation or deliver a lecture on the French Revolution, the words come out exactly as I intend them to. I don't get jumbled up or forget what I was trying to say halfway through a sentence. It’s just the *desire* to speak, the energy required to initiate the talking, that’s missing. But once I’m talking, the track is perfectly clear. I don't go off on strange tangents or find myself unable to string a coherent sentence together. 

I suppose the only thing is that I might be a little slower to respond sometimes, just because I'm sitting there trying to find the willpower to open my mouth, like with Brenda's phone calls. But that's not a matter of my thoughts being disorganized. It's just... a heavy silence, really. But when I do speak, no, I believe I'm as clear and organized as I've always been.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had any similar experiences like this earlier in your life, before the last four months?
turns.patient_response:
Before the last four months? Oh, heavens no. No, absolutely not. I have always been a very grounded person, rooted entirely in facts and reality—which, as I was just saying, makes perfect sense for a history teacher. turns.doctor_question: Have you experienced any major stress or upsetting life event around the time these symptoms began?
turns.patient_response:
Well, stress... it depends on how you define a stressful event, doesn't it? It wasn't a sudden, terrible tragedy, like a car accident or a sudden illness, but it was a very profound life transition. You see, my youngest child... well, he finally packed up and moved out. We drove him up to his university—this was about a year and two months ago, late August of last year. We helped him move all his boxes into his dormitory, set up his little mini-fridge, made sure he had all his supplies, and then... well, then I had to drive back home. It was just such a massive adjustment. You spend over two decades with your entire routine dictated by your children—their meals, their extracurriculars, their needs—and then suddenly, the nest is completely empty. I remember walking into his bedroom the day after we got back, and it was just spotless, which it never, ever was when he lived there, and I felt this immense, heavy weight settle over me. turns.doctor_question: Do you ever feel that your thoughts are being put into your mind by someone else, or taken out of your mind?
turns.patient_response:
Thoughts being put into my mind? Or taken out? Oh, no, no, it’s nothing like that. It isn't like some science fiction movie where someone is tampering with my brain or stealing my memories. My thoughts are entirely my own, I assure you. I know exactly what I am thinking. 

But... well, it’s more about what my thoughts are *focusing* on, what I am perceiving around me that no one else seems to grasp. In fact, the main reason I finally decided I needed to come in and talk to someone is because I absolutely cannot shake this feeling about the communications at the school. 

Every morning, I get to my classroom around 7:15, well before the first bell, and I open my computer to check the staff emails. And then, at 8:05, the morning announcements come on over the loudspeaker for the homeroom period. But lately, for these past few months, I have this overwhelming conviction that certain staff emails and those morning announcements are actually coded messages specifically about me. 

It sounds absurd when I say it out loud, I know it does, because I am a logical person. But when I'm sitting there reading a seemingly mundane email from the administration about, say, hallway pass procedures or faculty meeting agendas, I can read between the lines and see that it’s actually a disguised message directed entirely at me. I've even brought it up at work. I went next door to Sarah—she teaches sophomore English—and I showed her one of the emails, trying to explain the hidden meaning I was seeing. And she was so sweet, she very gently turned her monitor around and showed me her own inbox to prove that the exact same message was sent to the entire staff directory. She was trying to be helpful, gently showing me that everyone got it, that it was just a mass email. 

But even seeing it right there on her screen... it didn't change anything for me. I just couldn't shake the feeling that the message was still secretly meant for me, like I was the only one supposed to understand the real meaning behind the words. It just completely takes over my mind, trying to decode what they are saying about me in those announcements, even when all the logical evidence says otherwise. So, no one is putting thoughts into my head, but my mind is just entirely consumed by these messages.

turns.doctor_question: Do you feel that the emails or announcements are sending you personally special messages in a way that seems impossible or clearly unreal, or do they feel more like ordinary messages that just happen to be about you?

Well, that is the crux of the whole issue, isn't it? That's exactly why I finally made the appointment to come in. Because... logically, my rational brain—the brain that has a master's degree in education and has taught history for nearly thirty years—knows it seems impossible. I mean, how could the principal, Mr. Davis, possibly be encoding a secret message just for me in a mundane bulletin about the new tardy policy or the fire drill schedule? It sounds like something out of a Cold War spy novel, doesn't it? 

But when I am actually sitting there, reading the words on the screen or listening to the PA system... they don't feel like ordinary messages at all. They feel incredibly intricate, very deliberate, and specifically designed for me to decipher. 

Like, for example, just last Tuesday, the morning announcements came on—you know, the little chime plays over the loudspeaker, that 'ding-ding-dong' sound—and the student council president was reading off the cafeteria menu and the upcoming pep rally schedule. And she used the phrase, "Make sure to bring your spirit and stay in line." And I just... I felt it in my bones. I knew that "stay in line" wasn't about the students at the pep rally. It was a directive for me. It felt like a very special, personal warning about my behavior, or my thoughts... I don't even fully know what the ultimate goal of it is. 

And then with the emails... it's just like I was telling you about Sarah. When she so gently turned her monitor around to show me her inbox, my eyes saw the proof. I saw that the exact same email, word for word, was sent to the entire 'Staff-All' distribution list. A completely ordinary, mass-produced staff email. But my mind just couldn't accept it as ordinary. I just kept thinking, "Yes, Sarah received it too, but she doesn't *see* the real message." The hidden meaning was still right there, woven into the text, meant only for my eyes to understand. 

So, I suppose to answer your question... to everyone else, they are just ordinary messages. And a part of me knows it sounds completely unreal. But I just can’t shake the feeling that they are really coded messages about me. Even when my colleagues gently show me they were sent to everyone, that unshakable conviction just completely overrides my logic. It’s exhausting, really, trying to read between the lines of every single thing all morning long.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes an unshakable conviction that mundane school announcements and mass emails contain hidden, coded messages specifically directed at them, despite recognizing the logical impossibility and seeing evidence to the contrary.

turns.doctor_question: When these experiences happen, do you ever become confused or disorganized in your thinking or speech?
turns.patient_response:
Well, disorganized... I suppose that’s a very good word for it, though it feels more like my brain just suddenly shifts onto a completely different track without my permission. I mean, I don't forget where I am or who I am, but my actions and my words just get completely derailed. 

For instance, I was telling you about my lessons, and we also have these planning committees—like right now, we are organizing the spring art fair and history exhibition, which is a huge undertaking because it combines the two departments and requires a lot of logistical planning. And lately, during those art-fair meetings, or even right in the middle of a history lesson, I’ll just... catch myself stopping completely mid-task. I’ll be right in the middle of explaining a concept or assigning a task, and I’ll look down at my desk, and I will just start rearranging the dry-erase markers or the stacks of handouts. But I'm not just tidying them up, mind you. I have to put them in a very, very particular pattern. The blue marker has to be exactly parallel to the red one, the papers have to be fanned out at a specific angle... and I’ll just be entirely focused on doing that, completely ignoring the lesson.

And with my speech, it happens too. Sometimes, instead of responding normally when someone speaks to me, I’ll just repeat a phrase they just said. A student will ask a question, or one of the other teachers will make a suggestion at the meeting, and instead of answering, I’ll just echo their exact words back to them. Like a parrot, just repeating the end of their sentence out loud. 

And then there's this awful, heavy pause in the room, and I snap out of it and I feel so incredibly embarrassed. I know it completely interrupts what I’m supposed to be doing. I’m supposed to be leading the classroom or contributing to the committee, and instead, I’m sitting there lining up office supplies and repeating people's words back to them. It’s just so unlike me. I’ve spent thirty years commanding a classroom, and now I just get caught in these strange little loops that make my whole thought process feel terribly jumbled.
